newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Orogen, Oil Search fall on PNG crisis.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Orogen, Oil Search fall on PNG crisis.

text.p: Shares in Papua New Guinea (PNG) resources companies Orogen Minerals Ltd and Oil Search Ltd fell slightly in tentative early afternoon trade on Monday after reports emerged that the army and police had demanded the PNG government's resignation.
Brokers said political uncertainty had forced limited selling, but many were awaiting further more concrete developments before taking any more wholesale action.
"The PNG stocks are a bit weak as a knee-jerk reaction to the uncertainty," said Intersuisse head of equities Andrew Sekely.
Orogen Minerals, which is 51 percent owned by the PNG government, had fallen 11 cents to A$3.36 by 2.05 p.m. (0305 GMT) from its A$3.47 high just before the news emerged on volume of 56,800.
Oil Search's shares fell five cents to A$2.76 from its A$2.81 level just before the news and was down eight cents on the day.
Niugini Mining Ltd's shares were unchanged at A$3.05 while Lihir Gold was down one cent at A$2.24.
Bougainville Copper Ltd shares fell to 55 cents from 60 cents on two trades totalling 10,000 shares.
After the initial selling, comments emerged from senior military officials that a coup was not in progress.
"Let me assure you that we do not intend to have any coup, I can guarantee you that," Brigadier General Jerry Singirok said on Kalang FM radio in Port Moresby.

Australian Broadcasting Corporation radio reported earlier that the army and police had revolted and had called on the South Pacific nation's governor-general to sack the government over the hiring of mercenaries to help quell the long-running rebellion on Bougainville Island.
It was also reported that Singirok had said the foreign mercenaries in the country had been detained and would be expelled.
Defence force chief of staff Jack Tuat told Reuters that Singirok had visited the governor-general but was unable to say what had been discussed.
Brokers said the appearance of instability was the factor depressing share prices rather than concrete signs of a coup or a loss of government control.
"It's instability which is causing the selling rather than anything else," Sekely said.
